analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to test and report how their automated decision systems affect consumers in areas like housing, credit, and health care.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Yvette Clarke with 39 Democratic cosponsors, never got a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require large companies that use computer algorithms to make important decisions about people — whether they get a job, an apartment, a mortgage, insurance, or health care — to regularly study and report how those systems work and whether they harm or discriminate against consumers. The Federal Trade Commission would write the rules, enforce them (with help from state attorneys general), and publish a public, searchable record of where these systems are used and how consumers can appeal a decision.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose lives are shaped by automated decisions — job applicants, renters, mortgage and credit applicants, insurance buyers, patients. The bill would require companies to test their systems for bias and errors, try to fix likely harms, and give consumers ways to contest or appeal decisions. It would also create a public repository so people and researchers can see which automated systems are being used on them and how to seek recourse, and it would build a Bureau of Technology at the FTC so the agency has in-house technical experts. People affected by discrimination — which the bill specifically requires companies to test for across race, sex, age, disability, family status, and income — stand to benefit most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers judged by automated decision systems

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered companies to run ongoing impact assessments of any automated decision system used in a 'critical decision' — access to or cost of education, employment, utilities, financial services, health care, housing, legal services, and more — before and after deployment, and to try to eliminate or mitigate likely material harms [S3].

Requires companies to test for differential performance by consumers' race, sex, age, disability, religion, family status, socioeconomic status, and veteran status, and to document which harms they chose to leave unmitigated and why [S3].

Directs the FTC to build a publicly accessible, searchable repository of where automated decision systems are used, what data trained them, and how a consumer can contest, correct, or appeal a decision, updated quarterly [S3].

Enforces the rules through the FTC and lets state attorneys general sue violators on behalf of their residents, and explicitly preserves stronger state and local laws rather than overriding them [S3].
Builds new technical capacity at the FTC — a Bureau of Technology with at least 50 staff and 25 additional enforcement personnel — so the agency can actually evaluate these systems [S3].
Applies only to larger entities (generally over $50 million in annual receipts or data on over 1 million consumers), so small businesses are largely spared the compliance work [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that use automated decision systems in critical decisions — large tech platforms, AI software vendors, and firms in lending, insurance, housing, employment screening, and health care — would bear the cost of impact assessments, record-keeping, annual summary reports, and system fixes, and could face FTC penalties or state lawsuits for violations. Some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers in prices, and taxpayers would fund the new FTC staff and repository. Consumers get no right to sue companies directly; enforcement runs through the FTC and state officials.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large companies using automated decision systems

drawbacks.text: The impact assessments themselves would stay confidential: the bill says nothing in it requires a company to share assessment contents with the FTC or the public, beyond a limited summary report, so the deepest scrutiny would happen behind closed doors [S3].

It is a paperwork-first approach — companies document harms and mitigation steps, but the bill does not itself ban any biased system; enforcement depends on FTC regulations and later actions, and the rules would not even take effect until two years after they are written, years after enactment [S3].

Compliance would cost covered companies real money — ongoing testing, stakeholder consultation, documentation, and annual reporting — and some of that could be passed on to consumers; small firms just under the size thresholds escape while slightly larger competitors absorb the burden [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — forcing companies to find and fix algorithmic bias before it costs someone a job, a home, or health care, and giving consumers a visible way to contest decisions — outweighs the compliance costs, which fall mostly on large companies. The honest weaknesses are that the bill regulates through documentation rather than bans, keeps the full assessments secret, and relies on an FTC that would need years and new staff to act. It is a disclosure-and-diligence law, not a ban on harmful algorithms.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a consumer protection subcommittee on day one, and neither ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette Clarke of New York introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2022 on February 3, 2022, joined by 32 initial colleagues and 39 House Democrats in total as cosponsors [S1, S4, S5].

That same day the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died in committee with no vote ever taken [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large tech platforms and other companies that use automated decision systems in lending, hiring, housing, insurance, and health care are better off: they avoid the compliance and testing costs and keep operating opaque systems without federal scrutiny. Consumers get no new protection from algorithmic bias.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported it, so the bill was one-sided from the start — though no vote was ever held to test the split.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and AI software developers
industries.note: They would have to run impact assessments, consult outside stakeholders, report annually to the FTC, and appear in a public repository of automated decision systems. Their interest in keeping how their systems decide — and what data trains them — off the public record runs against the bill's transparency for consumers.

industries.industry: Banks, mortgage lenders, insurers, landlords, and employers using algorithmic screening
industries.note: As covered entities making 'critical decisions' about credit, housing, employment, and health care, they would face testing for differential performance by race, sex, age, and income, plus obligations to offer consumers ways to contest decisions. These are exactly the industries where opaque algorithms have the biggest effect on people's lives.
Companies handling identifying information on more than 1 million consumers would be covered, and assessments must document where training data came from and whether consumers consented.

industries.industry: AI auditing, privacy, and compliance services
industries.note: The bill requires independent auditing and stakeholder consultation as part of assessments, creating demand for third-party auditors and compliance tools.
